content: Crispin Adeniyi-Jones (1876–1957) was a medical director of Sierra Leonean heritage and the pioneering director of the Yaba Asylum in Nigeria. He later became one of Nigeria's leading nationalists, serving as a member and eventually the president of the Nigerian National Democratic Party (NNDP). He was also a long-standing member of Nigeria's legislative council, serving from 1923 to 1938. Beyond his political activities, he collaborated with Winifred Tete-Ansa of the National Congress of British West Africa to develop economic policies aimed at addressing emerging economic challenges in colonial West Africa. Crispin Adeniyi-Jones was born in Freetown, Sierra Leone. He received his secondary education at Sierra Leone Grammar School and pursued higher education at the University of Durham and the University of Dublin. He began his medical career at Rotunda Hospital in Dublin and later apprenticed under Sir Robert Boyce, a prominent physician from the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine. In 1904, he moved to Nigeria and joined the government medical services in Lagos. However, his initial enthusiasm was dampened by policies that restricted the advancement of African doctors and by financial constraints in many departments. Despite these challenges, he was appointed the first director of the Yaba Asylum, one of only two asylums in Nigeria at the time. In 1914, he left government service and established a successful private clinic in Lagos. On June 24, 1923, Adeniyi-Jones, along with Eric Moore, Egerton Shyngle, Herbert Macaulay, and Thomas Jackson, co-founded the Nigerian National Democratic Party (NNDP). The party leveraged a new initiative allowing elective representation in the legislative council and contested the three seats allocated to Africans in Lagos. Adeniyi-Jones won a seat in the council in 1923 and served for approximately 15 years. As a council member, he actively defended the interests of indigenous Africans, engaging in debates on major policy initiatives such as indirect rule and questioning colonial policies' benefits for Africans. He often opposed colonial policies that negatively impacted Nigerians and advocated for the advancement of Africans in the civil service. He also pushed for the establishment of more primary schools, the reduction of regional inequalities in cocoa grading, and the abolition of many provincial courts. Adeniyi-Jones played a significant role in economic development as a financier and president of several companies formed in the late 1920s and 1930s. He served as president of the Nigeria Mercantile Bank and was a major financier of the West African Cooperative Producers Limited. These companies were part of an ambitious economic program aimed at elevating the status of indigenous Africans within the British Empire. Before the 20th century, indigenous Nigerian groups were largely insulated from the global economy. However, the emergence of a colonial economic system in West Africa brought new challenges for African producers. Winifred Tete-Ansa, a Krobo man from the National Congress of British West Africa, proposed a plan to create African cooperatives as dominant business institutions in colonial Africa. Adeniyi-Jones supported this vision, financing ventures such as the West African Cooperative Producers and chairing the Nigeria Mercantile Bank. Although these ventures did not fully achieve their founders' aspirations, they laid a strong foundation for future initiatives. Notably, directors of the Nigeria Mercantile Bank, including A.A. Subair, later established the National Bank of Nigeria, which became the first successful indigenous bank in British West Africa.
